lessons.s1:
Tables, rows and columns

A relational database stores data in tables. A table is a grid: each row is one record, each column is one attribute with a fixed type. A table of employees might have id, name, role, dept_id and salary.

Why not a spreadsheet?

  • Types are enforced. A salary column holds numbers, not "about 120".
  • Relationships are explicit. dept_id points at a row in departments instead of repeating the department name in every row.
  • Concurrency. Many readers and writers, with transactions.

Seeing the shape

.tables        list the tables
.schema        show the columns of each table
SQL is declarative: you describe the result you want, not the steps to compute it. The database decides how to get there.
lessons.s2:
SELECT and WHERE

SELECT chooses columns, FROM chooses the table, WHERE filters rows.

SELECT * FROM employees;                       every column, every row
SELECT name, salary FROM employees;            two columns
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE role = 'engineer';
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > 100;
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE name LIKE 'A%';

Operators

  • = != > < >= <= — comparisons
  • LIKE '%text%' — pattern match; % is any run of characters
  • AND — both conditions must hold

Ordering and limiting

SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC;
SELECT name FROM employees ORDER BY name LIMIT 3;
Quote text with single quotes. salary = 100 compares a number; salary = '100' compares a string — the second will not match.
lessons.s4:
COUNT, SUM, AVG and GROUP BY

Aggregates collapse many rows into one value.

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees;          how many rows
SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees;       one number
SELECT MIN(salary), MAX(salary) FROM employees;

Grouping

GROUP BY runs the aggregate once per distinct value of a column:

SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*), AVG(salary)
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id;

That answers "how many people and what is the average pay, per department" in one query.

The rule that trips everyone up

Every column in the SELECT list must either be inside an aggregate or appear in GROUP BY. Otherwise the database has no single value to show for it.

Aggregates ignore NULL. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-null values — they differ when data is missing.
lessons.s6:
INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE

Reading is safe. Writing changes state, so the WHERE clause matters more than anywhere else.

INSERT INTO employees (id, name, role, dept_id, salary)
VALUES (6, 'Barbara', 'engineer', 1, 100);

UPDATE employees SET salary = 100 WHERE name = 'Grace';

DELETE FROM employees WHERE name = 'Linus';

The habit that saves you

Before an UPDATE or DELETE, run the same WHERE as a SELECT:

SELECT * FROM employees WHERE name = 'Linus';   -- 1 row? good
DELETE FROM employees WHERE name = 'Linus';

If the SELECT returns more rows than you expected, your condition is wrong — and you just avoided deleting the wrong data.

No WHERE means every row

DELETE FROM employees;   -- empties the table
There is no undo in this lab, and in production the safety net is a transaction plus a backup — not a second chance.
